title: Quiz: Chapman-Kolmogorov Equations and Stationary Distributions

questions.text: The Chapman-Kolmogorov equation P_{ij}^{(m+r)} = Σ_k P_{ik}^{(m)} · P_{kj}^{(r)} says:
options: The process must pass through every state k on the way from i to j
You sum over all possible intermediate states k at an intermediate time, capturing every possible path from i to j
The matrix product P · P is not a valid operation for stochastic matrices
Time-homogeneity is required for any n-step probability to exist
questions.explanation: The CK equation says: to go from state i in m+r steps to state j, the process passes through some intermediate state k after m steps. Summing over all k accounts for every possible path through the state space. The process does not visit every state — it visits exactly one intermediate state k, but we do not know which one, so we sum over all possibilities.

questions.text: For a time-homogeneous Markov chain, the 5-step transition probability matrix P^(5) equals:
options: P + P + P + P + P (the sum of five copies of P)
P raised to the power 5 using matrix multiplication
The 5th eigenvalue of P arranged into a matrix
questions.explanation: By the theorem proved in this lesson (by induction from the CK equation), the n-step transition matrix P^(n) equals the matrix P multiplied by itself n times: P^n. For n=5 this is P·P·P·P·P using matrix multiplication. Options (a) and (b) confuse matrix exponentiation with scalar multiplication; option (d) is not a defined operation.

questions.text: A stationary distribution π satisfies πP = π, and it is required that all entries of π are strictly positive.
questions.explanation: False. The requirements for a stationary distribution are: (1) πP = π and (2) all entries are non-negative and sum to 1. Some entries can be zero — for example, if a chain has absorbing states or communicating classes that cannot be escaped. Strict positivity of all entries is a property of ergodic chains, not of stationary distributions in general.

questions.text: We want P(sick at month 12 | patient was healthy at month 0). If state 0 = Healthy and state 1 = Sick, we compute:
options: One minus the (0,0) entry of P^12
questions.explanation: We need the 12-step transition probability from state 0 to state 1, which is P_{01}^{(12)} = [P^12]_{01} — the (row 0, column 1) entry of P raised to the 12th power. Option (a) incorrectly scales the one-step probability. Option (c) gives the probability of NOT being healthy at month 12, which includes dead patients as well as sick ones. Option (d) reverses the direction.

questions.text: A stable stochastic matrix is one where all rows are identical (each row equals the stationary distribution π).
questions.explanation: True. When a regular chain converges, P^n → π̃ where π̃ is a matrix with every row equal to the stationary distribution π. This matrix is called the stable matrix. The identical-rows property captures the long-run independence from starting state: after many steps, the probability of being in state j is π_j regardless of where you started.
